name: A. E. Perry
bio: Dr. Albert E. Perry was vice-president of the Union County NAACP in Monroe, North Carolina, and a close ally of Robert F. Williams. Shortly after he helped lead a campaign to desegregate Monroe's municipal swimming pool, he was charged and convicted of performing an abortion — a prosecution the NAACP denounced as a frame-up in retaliation for his civil-rights work.
charges: Performing an abortion — denounced by the NAACP as a frame-up for his desegregation work
sentence: Convicted; the NAACP fought the case as political retaliation

name: Asbury Howard
bio: Asbury Howard was an international vice-president of the Mine, Mill & Smelter Workers Union and president of the Bessemer Voters League in Alabama. In January 1959 he was convicted for commissioning a billboard sign depicting a chained Negro praying for equal rights; fined $100 and given six months, he was beaten by a white mob as he left the courthouse and put on the Bessemer chain gang.
charges: Local 'scurrilous publication' / breach-of-peace ordinance — for a civil-rights protest sign
sentence: $100 fine and six months on the Bessemer chain gang

name: Asbury Howard Jr.
bio: Asbury Howard Jr., a Korean War veteran, was arrested on a disorderly-conduct charge after he was beaten defending his father — the Bessemer, Alabama labor and civil-rights leader Asbury Howard — from a white mob inside the courthouse. While the white attackers went free, he was sentenced in March 1959 to a year's imprisonment and a $100 fine and jailed with his father.
charges: Disorderly conduct — after being beaten defending his father at the courthouse
sentence: One year's imprisonment and a $100 fine

name: Calvin Woods
affiliation: Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights
bio: The Rev. Calvin Woods was a Birmingham pastor and a leader of the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights. In January 1959 he was sentenced to six months in jail and fined $500 for urging his congregation to stop riding the city's Jim Crow buses.
charges: Inciting a bus boycott — urging his congregation to stop riding segregated buses
sentence: Six months in jail and a $500 fine

name: Septima Clark
bio: Septima Clark was the director of education at the Highlander Folk School, the interracial labor and civil-rights training center at Monteagle, Tennessee. She was arrested in the July 31, 1959 police raid on the school — on pretext liquor charges — part of a state campaign to shut down a place resented for its work on integration.
charges: Illegal possession of liquor — a pretext charge in the raid to close the interracial Highlander school
convicted: Arrested July 31, 1959; released on bond; faced grand-jury action
sentence: Arrested in the Highlander raid; charges fought as harassment

name: Guy Carawan
bio: Guy Carawan was the music director of the Highlander Folk School — the man who popularized 'We Shall Overcome' as the anthem of the civil-rights movement. He was arrested in the July 31, 1959 police raid on the interracial school on a pretext charge of drunkenness, part of the state's drive to close Highlander.
charges: Drunkenness — a pretext charge in the raid on the interracial Highlander school
sentence: Arrested in the Highlander raid; charges fought as harassment

name: Brent Barksdale
bio: Brent Barksdale was a teacher at the Highlander Folk School, arrested in the July 31, 1959 police raid on the interracial Monteagle, Tennessee school and charged with drunkenness and resisting arrest — pretext charges in a campaign to shut down a center long attacked as a hotbed of 'integration and communism.'
charges: Drunkenness / resisting arrest — pretext charges in the Highlander raid
sentence: Arrested in the Highlander raid; charges fought as harassment

name: Perry Sturges
bio: Perry Sturges was a teacher at the Highlander Folk School, arrested in the July 31, 1959 police raid on the interracial school at Monteagle, Tennessee and charged with drunkenness and resisting arrest — pretext charges that were part of the state's effort to revoke Highlander's charter and close it down.
charges: Drunkenness / resisting arrest — pretext charges in the Highlander raid
sentence: Arrested in the Highlander raid; charges fought as harassment

name: Theodore Gibson
bio: The Rev. Theodore R. Gibson was president of the Miami branch of the NAACP, cited for contempt by the Florida Legislative Investigating Committee (the segregationist 'Johns Committee') in December 1959 for refusing to bring the branch's membership lists to its hearings. His resistance led to the landmark Gibson v. Florida Legislative Investigation Committee.
charges: Contempt of the Florida Legislative Investigating ('Johns') Committee — refusing to produce NAACP membership lists
sentence: Cited for contempt; fought the anti-NAACP probe to the Supreme Court

name: A. Leon Lowry
bio: The Rev. A. Leon Lowry of Tampa was the Florida state president of the NAACP. In December 1959 the Florida Legislative Investigating Committee — the 'Johns Committee' — recommended that he be jailed for contempt for failing to appear before its segregation-era probe of the NAACP.
charges: Contempt of the Florida Legislative Investigating ('Johns') Committee
convicted: Committee recommended he be jailed for contempt (1959)
sentence: Faced jailing for contempt; resisted the anti-NAACP probe

name: Lawrence Gore
bio: Lawrence Gore was a Textile Workers Union organizer convicted in August 1959 in the Henderson, North Carolina strike case — the prosecution of union men for an alleged conspiracy to dynamite the struck Harriet-Henderson cotton mills. The union condemned the case as a frame-up built on the testimony of a paid informer. He was sentenced to six to ten years.
charges: Conspiracy to dynamite the struck Harriet-Henderson mills — condemned by the union as a frame-up

name: Charles Auslander
bio: Charles Auslander was a Textile Workers Union organizer convicted with Boyd Payton and Lawrence Gore in the Henderson, North Carolina strike case (1959), charged with conspiracy to dynamite the struck mills. At sentencing the judge pointed to his being an outsider — 'the union sent you' — underscoring the union's charge that the case was an anti-labor frame-up. He drew six to ten years.
charges: Conspiracy to dynamite the struck Harriet-Henderson mills — condemned by the union as a frame-up
